title: Johns Hopkins LSTM click detector lets a man with ALS spell 10.2 characters a minute for 90 days without retraining
summary: A click detector built on a long short-term memory network let a man with ALS spell through a brain implant at a median 10.2 characters per minute for 90 days without retraining, in the laboratory.
account: A participant with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) in a clinical trial at Johns Hopkins (NCT03567213) had a chronically implanted high-density electrocorticographic brain-computer interface over sensorimotor cortex. High-gamma power vectors from 128 channels fed a long short-term memory layer with 25 hidden units and fully connected layers. These classified rest versus grasp every 100 milliseconds. The click detector was trained on almost 44 minutes of data (480 trials) collected up to 21 days before use. It then ran for 90 days without retraining. The participant controlled a switch-scanning speller for a total of 626 minutes with a median spelling rate of 10.2 characters per minute. The team posted the work as a preprint on 25 September 2023. Candrea et al. published it in Communications Medicine on 22 October 2024. The paper states that all data collection and testing were performed in the laboratory. No home use is reported. In a preprint posted on 3 October 2025, the Johns Hopkins and UMC Utrecht team behind the click detector reported that offline gesture decoding in a man with ALS in this trial worsened over five months, starting about two years after implant. A systematic review by Swanson and colleagues (Journal of Neural Engineering, 23 June 2026) records the study as running 12 weeks without recalibration. The review's first author also lists UMC Utrecht.

The participant controlled a switch-scanning speller for a total of 626 minutes with a median spelling rate of 10.2 characters per minute. The team posted the work as a preprint on 25 September 2023. Candrea et al. published it in Communications Medicine on 22 October 2024. The paper states that all data collection and testing were performed in the laboratory. No home use is reported. In a preprint posted on 3 October 2025, the Johns Hopkins and UMC Utrecht team behind the click detector reported that offline gesture decoding in a man with ALS in this trial worsened over five months, starting about two years after implant. A systematic review by Swanson and colleagues (Journal of Neural Engineering, 23 June 2026) records the study as running 12 weeks without recalibration. The review's first author also lists UMC Utrecht.
